title: Direct and control livestock health care activities

lessons.title: Planning the herd health programme
lessons.html:
Planning the herd health programme

At supervisor level you are no longer only giving treatments - you direct the team that does them and control the whole health programme against the plan agreed with the farm's veterinarian.

Working with the vet

The herd health plan should be written with the vet and reviewed at least once a year. It sets out:

  • The vaccination schedule for each class of animal and when it falls in the farming calendar.
  • Internal and external parasite control strategy, including monitoring (faecal egg counts, FAMACHA, tick counts) and product rotation to slow resistance.
  • Mineral and lick programme.
  • Biosecurity rules for buying in, quarantine, visitors and vehicles.
  • Which diseases are monitored, and which must be reported to the state vet under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.
  • Treatment protocols for common conditions the team may treat without calling the vet, and when the vet must be called.

Turning the plan into schedules

Break the plan into monthly schedules showing which group is treated, with what, by whom, and the resources required. Book the vet for tasks that require one, such as pregnancy diagnosis, breeding soundness tests or brucellosis testing.

Remedy stock control

Keep a remedy register: product, batch, expiry, quantity in and out, who used it and on which animals. Store remedies locked, at the temperature the label requires. Vaccine fridges need a thermometer that is checked and recorded daily. Order ahead of the schedule so that treatments are never delayed. Use first-expiry stock first and dispose of expired stock according to the label.

Budget

Estimate the cost per animal of the health programme and compare it with actual spending each month. Unexpected increases often point to an outbreak, wastage or poor dose calibration.

lessons.title: Directing the team during health operations
lessons.html:
Directing the team during health operations

Briefing before work

Before a dipping, vaccination or dosing day, brief the team on: the animals to be worked, the products and doses, each person's role (bringing in, working the race, dosing, injecting, recording), safety points, and what to do with animals that look sick. Check that PPE and first aid kit are on site.

Allocating roles

Give injections and dose calibration only to workers who have been trained and assessed. Pair new workers with experienced ones. Rotate tiring jobs such as working the race to prevent fatigue-related injuries.

Quality checks during the work

  • Check dosing gun calibration at the start and every so often during the work by dispensing into a measuring cylinder.
  • Watch injection technique and needle changes.
  • Check that every animal is marked and none is missed or treated twice.
  • Compare the number of animals worked with the record sheet and the stock register.
  • Check the dip tank level and strength as the label and farm procedure require.

Animal welfare and handling

Do not allow beating, tail twisting or dogs in the race. Keep group sizes manageable. Give animals water and shade if they wait long in the kraal. These are requirements of the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962, and calm animals are also safer to treat.

Safety controls

Conduct a risk assessment for each health operation: crush injuries, kicks, needle-stick, chemical exposure, heat. Put controls in place and make sure they are followed. Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, injuries must be reported and investigated. Keep the product labels on site so medical staff can see them if someone is exposed.

Closing the work

Clean and store equipment, return remedies to the store, update the remedy register and treatment records the same day.

lessons.title: Monitoring outcomes and managing outbreaks
lessons.html:
Monitoring outcomes and managing outbreaks

Is the programme working?

Review health indicators regularly with the manager and the vet:

IndicatorWhat it may show
Mortality by age and causeGaps in vaccination, predators, nutrition
Abortion rateBrucellosis, other infectious causes, nutrition
Faecal egg counts after dosingWorm resistance to the product
Tick burdens after dippingWrong concentration or resistance
Treatment numbers and costDisease pressure and wastage

Ask the vet for post-mortem examinations of unexplained deaths. Store samples as instructed.

Recognising an outbreak

Several animals sick with similar signs in a short time, sudden deaths, or signs of a controlled disease (for example blisters in the mouth and feet suggesting foot-and-mouth disease) must be treated as a possible outbreak.

First response

  1. Stop movement of animals on and off the farm.
  2. Isolate sick animals and keep people and dogs away from carcasses.
  3. Call the farm vet and, for suspected controlled diseases, the state veterinarian.
  4. Record what you have seen and when.
  5. Follow official instructions on quarantine, vaccination and disposal exactly.

Residue and food safety control

Check that no animal leaves for slaughter and no milk is sold within a withdrawal period. Audit records against movements before each sale.

Continuous improvement

After each season, review what went well and what did not, update protocols, and retrain the team where needed.

Key points

  • Base the health programme on a written plan with the vet.
  • Control remedy stock, storage and expiry with a register.
  • Brief the team, allocate trained people and check quality during the work.
  • Use indicators to judge whether the programme works.
  • In a suspected outbreak, stop movements, isolate and call the vet and state vet.
